claims.text: The Group IV–V RHEA can be fabricated by SEBM using a pre-alloyed powder feedstock.
The initial elemental-powder blend has high oxygen/interstitial content and a coarse, heterogeneous, segregation-prone microstructure.
SEBM can employ a two-stage semi-sintering/melting process at about 920 °C build temperature, 50 μm layer thickness, and 80 mm/s beam speed.
The SEBM material should receive a two-stage vacuum anneal at 1000–1300 °C for 24 hours.
Rapid cooling should follow the high-temperature annealing treatment.
The proposed SEBM and annealing route will homogenize the alloy.
The proposed route will produce an ultrafine-grained BCC solid solution.
The resulting microstructure will suppress intermetallic precipitation.
The resulting microstructure will minimize segregation of interstitial impurities at grain boundaries.
SEBM intrinsically produces rapid solidification rates of 10^4–10^6 K/s.
Rapid solidification combined with high-temperature annealing dissolves brittle phases.
Rapid solidification combined with high-temperature annealing refines the grains.
Reducing grain size in polycrystalline BCC metals can improve plasticity, fatigue strength, and creep behavior.
Processing under vacuum prevents interstitial embrittlement.
Group IV–V mixing modifies the electronic structure and changes the elastic instability from tensile to shear failure, increasing intrinsic ductility.
The optimized route will significantly reduce porosity relative to non-optimized SEBM.
The processed alloy will retain high yield strength above 1000 °C.
The processed alloy will have better room-temperature ductility than a cast counterpart.
Preferential evaporation of lighter elements such as Ti or V during high-energy SEBM may alter stoichiometry and phase stability.
An interstitial content above 0.5 at% is a threshold for brittleness in this alloy.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis specifies a pre-alloyed powder feedstock, whereas the initial-state description specifies a blend of elemental powders.
